public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 477

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/477](https://www.erdosproblems.com/477)
- [Sek59](http://dml.cz/dmlcz/100376) Milan Sekanina, Замечания к фактoризации беcкoнечнoй цикличеcкoй группы, Czechoslovak Mathematical Journal, Vol. 9 (1959), No. 4, 485–495
- The resolution is recorded at [erdosproblems.com/477](https://www.erdosproblems.com/477), with a
  proof exposition by T. F. Bloom of a construction found independently by several provers.
-/

@[expose] public section

open Polynomial Set

namespace Erdos477

/--
Is there a polynomial $f:\mathbb{Z}\to \mathbb{Z}$ of degree at least $2$ and a set
$A\subset \mathbb{Z}$ such that for any $n\in \mathbb{Z}$ there is exactly one $a\in A$ and
$b\in \{ f(k) : k\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ such that $n=a+b$?

The answer is yes, contrary to the expectation of Erdős and Graham: such an `A` exists whenever
$f(n) = n^d$ for even $d \ge 6$.

The linked formal proof (Codex, following Price's exposition) exhibits a complement of
$\{k^6 : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$; it states uniqueness as `∃! p : ℤ × ℤ, p.1 ∈ A ∧ p.2 ∈ B ∧ p.1 + p.2 = n`
and the degree condition as `2 ≤ f.natDegree`.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 12, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos477.lean#L54"]
theorem erdos_477 : answer(True) ↔
    ∃ f : ℤ[X], 2 ≤ f.degree ∧ ∃ A : Set ℤ,
      ∀ z, ∃! ab ∈ A ×ˢ (Set.range f.eval), z = ab.1 + ab.2 := by
  sorry

/--
There is no such $A$ for the polynomial $f(x) = X^2$.

This is shown in [Sek59].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 12]
theorem erdos_477.variants.S_sq :
    letI f := X ^ 2
    ∀ A : Set ℤ, ∃ z, ¬ ∃! a ∈ A ×ˢ (Set.range f.eval), z = a.1 + a.2 := by
  sorry

/--
There is no such $A$ for any polynomial $f(x) = aX^2 + bX + c$, if $a | b$
with $a \ne 0$ and $b \ne 0$.
This was found be AlphaProof for the specific instance $X^2 - X + 1$ and then generalised.
 -/
@[category research solved, AMS 12]
theorem erdos_477.variants.degree_two_dvd_condition_b_ne_zero {a b c : ℤ} (ha : a ≠ 0) (hb : b ≠ 0)
    (hab : a ∣ b) :
    let f := a • X ^ 2 + b • X + C c
    ∀ A : Set ℤ, ∃ z, ¬ ∃! a ∈ A ×ˢ (Set.range f.eval), z = a.1 + a.2 := by
  sorry

/--
Probably there is no such $A$ for the polynomial $X^3$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 12]
theorem erdos_477.variants.X_pow_three :
    letI f := X ^ 3
    ∀ A : Set ℤ, ∃ z, ¬ ∃! a ∈ A ×ˢ (Set.range f.eval), z = a.1 + a.2 := by
  sorry

/--
Sekanina [Sek59] asked whether there is no such $A$ for $X^k$, for every $k \ge 2$.
This is false: a complement exists for every even $k \ge 6$. The linked formal proof gives the
case $k = 6$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 12, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos477.lean#L42"]
theorem erdos_477.variants.monomial : answer(False) ↔
    ∀ (k : ℕ), 2 ≤ k →
      letI f := X ^ k
      ∀ A : Set ℤ, ∃ z, ¬ ∃! a ∈ A ×ˢ (Set.range f.eval), z = a.1 + a.2 := by
  sorry

end Erdos477

reformulations.difference: The source asks for a 'polynomial f: ℤ → ℤ' (which could include integer-valued polynomials with rational coefficients) of degree at least 2. The Lean takes f : ℤ[X] and writes the degree condition as `2 ≤ f.degree` in WithBot ℕ. 'Exactly one a ∈ A and b ∈ {f(k)}' becomes `∃! ab ∈ A ×ˢ Set.range f.eval, z = ab.1 + ab.2`, i.e. uniqueness of the pair of summand values, not of the input k.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: `2 ≤ f.degree ↔ 2 ≤ f.natDegree`: f = 0 fails both, and otherwise degree = natDegree. The ∃!-over-pairs form is exactly the source's 'exactly one a and b'; Tao's forum comment confirms that pairs (a, f(n)) are what is counted. I proved in Lean that the file's right-hand side is equivalent to the linked proof's `OriginalStatement` (natDegree form, `∃! p, p.1 ∈ A ∧ p.2 ∈ B ∧ p.1 + p.2 = n`). Restricting to ℤ[X] only strengthens the existential. The recorded resolution has witness X^6 ∈ ℤ[X] (formally proved at the linked L54), so the Lean right-hand side is true and implies the source's. `answer(True) ↔ RHS` is therefore correct under either reading of 'polynomial f: ℤ → ℤ'.

reformulations.difference: Sekanina's question about k-th powers is encoded as one universal statement, `answer(False) ↔ ∀ k ≥ 2, no complement exists for Set.range (X^k).eval`. This takes the k-th powers over all of ℤ, which for odd k is larger than the set of nonnegative k-th powers the historical sources probably meant.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The universal claim is refuted by a single k. At k = 6 (even), {n^6 : n ∈ ℤ} = {n^6 : n ≥ 0}. Complements exist for {n^6 : n ≥ 0} (Price's claim, d ≥ 5) and for {n^6 : n ≥ 1} (Bloom's exposition, d ≥ 5). So the answer to 'is there no complement for every k ≥ 2?' is 'no' whichever set of k-th powers is meant, and `answer(False)` is correct. I proved in Lean that the linked sixth-power tiling (L42) implies the file's statement.

could_not_verify: Erdos477.erdos_477.variants.S_sq and Erdos477.erdos_477.variants.monomial: the docstrings attribute the X^2 result and the k-th power question to Sekanina [Sek59]. The dml.cz PDF is a CCITT-scanned Russian paper with no text layer, the sandbox has no PDF/OCR tools, and the zbMATH review does not mention k-th powers. So I could not check Sekanina's exact wording, including whether his k-th powers range over ℤ or over n ≥ 0. The truth values are settled anyway: I proved S_sq in Lean, and monomial's answer(False) holds in every reading.

Erdos477.erdos_477.variants.X_pow_three: no accessible source states the X^3 conjecture explicitly. The Erdős–Graham book (ErGr80, p. 95) was not accessible. The wording 'Probably there is no such A for X^3' matches the pre-2026 erdosproblems remark 'Probably there is no such A for any polynomial f' applied to f = X^3. I judge the statement faithful as the X^3 case of the site's current problem (k ∈ ℤ), and still open: neither proof claim covers d = 3.
review.notes:
No misformalizations found. What I checked:
(1) #print shows every statement elaborates as intended: `X ^ k : ℤ[X]`; `f.eval` is `fun x => eval x f`; `∃! ab ∈ S, P` means `∃! ab, ab ∈ S ∧ P`; the degree-two `let` is the polynomial a·x² + b·x + c, confirmed with a Lean `↔`.
(2) I proved `variants.S_sq` and `variants.degree_two_dvd_condition_b_ne_zero` in Lean, sorry-free with standard axioms only, and checked each proof against the file's exact statement with `type_of%`. So these solved variants are correctly stated. The `a ∣ b` hypothesis is unnecessary but harmless.
(3) The linked formal proofs: L54 `erdos_477 : OriginalStatement` is equivalent to the file's right-hand side (proved in Lean), and L42 `erdos477_sixth_power` implies `variants.monomial` with answer(False) (proved in Lean). The linked repository (155 files) has no sorry, no axiom declarations and no native_decide, and does not shadow standard names. I did not compile it (it is pinned to Lean v4.33.0).
(4) Status: the site records the problem SOLVED (yes), with complements for f(n) = n^d for all even d ≥ 6. This matches `answer(True)`, `research solved` and the docstrings. X^3 over ℤ is covered by neither proof claim (Price: d ≥ 5 with n ≥ 0; pipeline-math: d = 13 over ℤ), and the site's degree-2 obstruction does not apply to it, so `research open` is right.
Minor, not reported: the docstring typo 'found be AlphaProof', and some Latin letters mixed into the Cyrillic title of Sek59.
